claims.text: OpenAI reports that Codex code review comments on 36% of PRs generated entirely by Codex cloud, and 46% of those comments result in the author making a code change, versus 53% for comments on human-generated PRs.
OpenAI reports that authors address reviewer comments with a code change in 52.7% of cases, and over 80% of comment reactions are positive.
As of October 2025, OpenAI's Codex code reviewer handles more than 100k external PRs per day.

OpenAI found that giving a GPT-5 reviewer repository access and code execution made it a stronger reviewer, catching more critical issues with fewer false alarms than a diff-only reviewer; dedicated code-review training improved results further.
OpenAI deliberately accepted modestly reduced recall in exchange for high precision and developer trust in its code reviewer, optimizing signal-to-noise first.

In OpenAI's controlled study, a reviewer at a small fraction of the generator's token spend caught a large share of previously identified high-severity issues; extra inference budget mostly improved calibration and reduced false alarms.

OpenAI observed that reviewer recall on known bugs was consistently higher for human-written code than for Codex-generated code, and that performance dropped more rapidly with lower thinking budget on model-generated code.
OpenAI's recall evaluation is limited because its test set contains only issues humans already identified, so it cannot validate new findings the reviewer makes with more time.
OpenAI warns that over-reliance is a risk: teams may treat a clean automated review as a guarantee of safety rather than one defense layer.

OpenAI argues that training-time verifiers (reward models) should be over-sensitive and may use task-specific information, while deployed reviewers must prioritize precision and user trust, so a single verifier should not serve both roles.

In a controlled experiment with 30 artifacts, 150 planted errors, 10 review conditions and 900 review sessions, a top-tier cross-model reviewer (GPT-5.4) was not significantly different in F1 from same-model review in a fresh session (CCR), which does not establish equivalence.
Cross-model review and same-model fresh-session review found partly different planted errors, with a Jaccard overlap of 41.2%.

At two review calls, one same-model fresh-session review plus one cross-model review matched 56.7% of planted errors versus 42.7% for two same-model reviews (Holm-adjusted p=.006), but not significantly more than two top-tier cross-model reviews, so model difference and reviewer capability are not separated.
A lightweight cross-model reviewer (Gemini 2.5 Flash) scored no higher than same-model review, and numerically below baseline same-context review.
Withholding requirements from the reviewer raised cross-model F1 by +2.2 and +3.0pp for the two lower-tier reviewers but not the top tier (-0.2pp), in untested point estimates.
Same-model fresh-session review (CCR) exceeded same-context self-review by only 1.5pp F1 (28.6% vs 27.1%, unadjusted p=0.26) after excluding one baseline run of uncertain provenance.
Pairwise finding overlap was 52.2% within the same model versus 37-46% across models, a descriptive comparison rather than a test of error correlation.

In the cross-model review study, 187 of 1,995 cross-model false positives (9.4%) were classified as model-bias errors, where the reviewer flags issues based on its own training rather than real defects.

Prior work cited in the cross-model study reports that in-context self-correction without external feedback degrades accuracy, and that evaluator LLMs miss quality drops in over 50% of cases on perturbed answers.
StrongDM describes end-to-end scenarios kept outside the codebase, like a holdout set in model training, as validation that is harder for a model to cheat.

On SWE-bench Verified, 29.6% of plausible patches from three issue-solving tools behaved differently from the developers' patches, and the weaknesses found inflated reported resolution rates by 6.4 percentage points on average.

UTBoost found that SWE-Bench's manually written test cases are often insufficient, allowing generated patches to pass without resolving the issue; after fixing the parser it identified 64 erroneous agent patches that had been counted as correct.

A passing LLM-generated unit test suite provides evidence only that code is correct with respect to the LLM's understanding, not the developer's; the ScenarioBench study of 30 Defects4J methods with expert-curated scenarios found such suites can give a false sense of security.
An empirical study of LLM-as-judge for patch correctness recommends using it as a triage aid that ranks candidates for human review rather than a replacement for it.
One comparative study reported transformer-based models reaching 87.3% average accuracy on security vulnerabilities but only 62.1% on subtle logic errors in automated code review.
